extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, and practicing scientists interested in foundations and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying how terms like cause, force, will, law, and motion should be defined and used in scientific discourse — distinguishing descriptive scientific statements from metaphysical or prescriptive ones. Aimed at guiding correct epistemological usage across scientific disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion as a scientific conception (not a perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion is a conception, rather than a perception — a scientific mode of representing change of sense-impressions, rather than a sense-impression itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'motion' in the scientific sense as an intellectual representation of sequences of sense-impressions; the chapter uses the term in its popular sense for sequences of sense-impressions but advises the reader of the conceptual status. (Footnote: see statement that 'motion' will be treated as a conception in the sequel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics and laws as concise descriptions of routines of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics (and scientific laws generally) aim at 'the complete description in the simplest possible manner' of such motions as occur in nature — i.e., concise descriptions of repeated sequences of our sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the laws of mechanics as descriptions of past repeated experience that permit confident expectation of future similar sequences; do not assume they reveal metaphysical necessity. Avoid contrasting mechanics with other sciences in principle — differences are quantitative (simplicity/generalness) not qualitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret scientific laws descriptively, not prescriptively (avoid 'prescriptive science')
rubrics_metrics.description: When we say we have a 'mechanical explanation' we mean we have described in the concise language of mechanics a certain routine of perceptions — not that we have discovered an inherent necessity enforcing that routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wording or thinking that scientific laws 'enforce' phenomena; explicitly mark laws as descriptions of 'how' (the routine) rather than answers to the 'why' (metaphysical enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Force should be understood as a measure of motion, not a metaphysical cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Force, when used as a name for a particular measure of motion, 'involves no obscurity' and is convenient, but defining force as the cause that necessitates change leads to metaphysical confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer interpreting forces (e.g., gravitation) as measures describing rate/changes of motion (how bodies move), not as original enforcers that explain 'why' motions occur; analyze statements like 'the law of gravitation causes bodies to fall' as descriptive rather than causal in a metaphysical sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish popular/metaphysical 'cause' (enforcement) from scientific 'cause' (routine of experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular usage often implies enforcement (a thing 'necessitates' an effect), whereas scientifically 'cause' should mark a stage in a routine of experience (uniform antecedence), not an inherent necessitating power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using 'cause' scientifically, restrict it to empirical regularities (stages in routines of perceptions). Explicitly flag and avoid confounding metaphysical language (first causes, enforcing wills/forces) with scientific descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat will as a legitimate scientific 'first cause'; treat acts of will as secondary causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Will appears only as a stage in a routine of perceptions (a secondary cause) and, although it may appear to originate motion, it does not provide a scientific necessity that enforces subsequent stages of the sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze acts of will as conditioned by physiological/psychological history (memory, training, inheritance, health) and therefore as describable stages within a routine; do not posit will as an arbitrary enforcer or scientifically explanatory first cause. Example: my act of will may start a stone's motion but cannot account for its continued motion (gravitation describes that part).

rubrics_metrics.name: First causes have no scientific standing; avoid inferring unobservable 'first causes'
rubrics_metrics.description: Science 'knows nothing of first causes' — positing them either imports metaphysics or simply labels the limit of our knowledge; they cannot be legitimately inferred from scientific investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering apparent explanatory gaps, prefer to state 'here ignorance begins' rather than invent first causes beyond sense-impression. Recognize claims of first causes as markers of a limit to knowledge, not as scientific conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define cause empirically by uniform antecedence (Millian formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a sequence of perceptions D, E, F, G is invariably preceded by the perception C (or C, D, E, F, G always occur in this order), C is said to be a cause of D, E, F, G — i.e., causation is uniform antecedence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical regularity and repetition as the basis for causal statements; illustrate with examples (number sequences) to distinguish empirical regularity from logical necessity. Cite John Stuart Mill's 'uniform antecedence' as consistent with this scientific concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical routine from logical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: No sequence of sense-impressions involves logical necessity as in geometry; scientific routines are matters of empirical repetition and probability, not logical deduction from concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast mathematical/geometrical necessities (e.g., angle in a semicircle is a right angle) with empirical regularities (e.g., numerical sequences observed repeatedly) to prevent conflating 'must' in logic with 'habitual' in experience. Emphasize probabilistic/empirical character of scientific inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of widening the term 'cause' into unmanageable historical chains
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of any individual thing can be widened into a description of the various past stages of the universe (e.g., causes of an ash-tree lead into geological and historical causes); such exhaustive tracing is impracticable and not the task of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit causal analysis to manageable, useful descriptions; recognize that while causes can be traced back indefinitely in principle, scientific practice should focus on effective, tractable causal descriptions rather than attempting to 'know the universe' by tracing every antecedent.
